passage: When an automated system fails and a human operator fails to rescue it, the official account usually ends with the words 'human error'. The phrase is accurate in a narrow sense, since a person did do the wrong thing, but it hides the way the situation was produced. Automation is typically introduced to take over the parts of a task that are routine and well understood. What remains for the human is whatever the designers could not automate: the rare, ambiguous, fast-moving situations in which the machine gives up or behaves strangely. The person is thus left with the hardest part of the job, and is expected to perform it suddenly, after long periods of doing almost nothing.

Those long periods matter. Skill at controlling a process is kept alive by exercising it, and an operator who has spent months watching a screen rather than flying, steering or adjusting will have less of it than one who did the work by hand. Worse, the automation removes the everyday experience through which people build an intuitive model of how the system behaves, so that when something goes wrong they must reason about it from first principles, under pressure, with alarms sounding. Monitoring is also something human beings do badly. Attention drifts when nothing happens for hours, and the more reliable the machine, the longer the stretches in which nothing happens.

The result is a curious inversion. The better the automation works in ordinary conditions, the less prepared its human supervisors may be for the extraordinary ones, and the more surprising their failure will look when it comes. Calling that failure human error locates the fault in the individual at the very moment when the design of the whole arrangement deserves scrutiny.

None of this is a case against automation, which has removed a great deal of tedium and many kinds of mistake. It is a case for designing automated systems around the people who must step in when they fail. That might mean having operators run the process manually at regular intervals so that their skill does not decay, building displays that show what the machine is doing and why rather than only whether it is working, or deciding deliberately that some tasks should remain shared even when they could be fully automated. Such measures cost efficiency in the short run. Their justification is that the moments they prepare for, although rare, are the ones in which the most is at stake.

passage: Public health suffers from a peculiar handicap: when it succeeds, nothing happens. A hospital can display the patients it has cured and a surgeon can point to the tumour she removed, but the officials who ran a vaccination campaign have nothing to show for their work except an absence. The measles outbreak that did not occur leaves no photographs, no grateful survivors and no line in the local newspaper. Success in prevention is a count of events that never took place, and such a count is always an estimate rather than an observation.

This invisibility is more than an inconvenience for those who would like credit. It changes how the public weighs risk. When a disease has been made rare, the vaccine against it becomes more noticeable than the disease itself. A parent who has never seen a child struggle to breathe with diphtheria, but who has heard about a neighbour's child running a fever after an injection, is weighing something vivid against something abstract. From where that parent stands, the calculation is not foolish; the danger really has receded from ordinary experience. What the parent may not see is that it receded because of the very programme now being doubted, and that it can return if enough people reach the same conclusion.

The same pattern appears wherever the benefit of a measure is an event that fails to happen. A food inspection service that keeps contaminated products off the shelves is easy to cut in a lean year, because the year after the cut looks much like the year before it. The costs of neglect arrive slowly, are spread thinly, and are usually blamed on something else by the time they become visible. Spending on treatment, by contrast, answers a need that is present and named. It is not surprising that budgets drift towards cure and away from prevention even when prevention is the cheaper way to buy the same health.

None of this means that the public should simply take officials at their word. Claims about disasters averted are claims about a world that did not happen, and they can be inflated by any agency that wants to protect its budget. The answer to invisibility is not deference but better ways of making the counterfactual visible: comparisons with places and periods that lacked the measure, honest accounting of the measure's own costs and side effects, and records kept carefully enough that a sceptic could check them. Prevention will never be as photogenic as rescue, but it can be made legible, and a public that can read its record is more likely to keep paying for it.

passage: Suppose the history of life could be rewound to some early point and allowed to run again. Would anything like the present living world appear a second time? One school answers no. Evolution, on this view, is a chain of contingencies, each step dependent on the particular steps before it and on unrepeatable accidents of climate, geology and mutation. Alter any early link, and the chain would run off in another direction entirely; the existence of vertebrates, of flowering plants or of our own species would be no more to be expected than a particular sequence of cards in a shuffled deck. The rival school points to the remarkable frequency with which evolution arrives at the same solution independently. Camera-like eyes have arisen separately in vertebrates and in octopuses; streamlined bodies have evolved in fish, in extinct marine reptiles and in dolphins; flight has been achieved by insects, pterosaurs, birds and bats. If the same designs keep recurring, the argument runs, the outcome of a second run would be broadly familiar.

Each school has a strong case, and each tends to treat the other's evidence as anecdote. Convergence enthusiasts can list hundreds of cases, but the list is assembled after the fact from the solutions that did recur, and it says nothing about the far larger number of forms that appeared once and never again. Contingency enthusiasts can point to those unrepeated forms, but they often treat the mere fact that a lineage had a particular history as proof that its outcome depended on that history, which does not follow: a ball may take a unique path down a hillside and still come to rest in the only hollow at the bottom.

Much of the disagreement, I want to suggest, dissolves once we notice that the two schools are describing life at different levels of detail. At the level of broad functional solutions, a second run would very probably produce organisms that see, swim, fly and filter food, because the physical problems of moving through water or air, or of forming an image from light, admit only a few good solutions. At the level of particular lineages, the replay would almost certainly differ: there is no reason to expect that the flying creatures would be birds, or that the swimmers would have backbones. Convergence is a claim about the space of workable designs; contingency is a claim about which occupants of that space history happens to supply. The two are compatible, and both are probably true.

This reconciliation has a cost, and it is worth stating plainly. If the question that matters is whether a replay would produce something like us, a self-aware animal that makes tools and uses language, then neither school's best evidence is decisive. Intelligence of our kind has arisen, so far as we know, only once, and a single case cannot reveal whether it was a likely destination or a fluke. The recurrence of eyes and wings tells us that some problems have few solutions; it does not tell us that every capacity we value is among those solutions. On the questions that most excite the public, the honest answer is that the evidence does not yet discriminate between the two views.

passage: Over the past few decades many voluntary organisations have come to manage their volunteers much as firms manage staff. There are role descriptions and application forms, induction sessions, supervisors and annual counts of hours given. The change is usually presented as simple progress. Volunteers who know what is expected of them are said to stay longer, and organisations that can report their hours to funders are better placed to win support. Funders, understandably, prefer measurable outputs, and organisations competing for limited grants have every incentive to supply them. Both claims are plausible, and neither is the whole story.

What the managerial model tends to forget is that volunteering was never only a cheaper form of labour. People who give their time without pay are also choosing what to do, with whom and on what terms, and that choice is part of what they value. A retired teacher who helped run a reading club because she liked the children and the other helpers may find, once the club has become a programme with targets and a coordinator, that she has been turned into an unpaid employee of something she no longer recognises. She has lost not her wages, which she never had, but her say. Many such volunteers do not complain; they simply drift away, and their departure is recorded, if at all, as a problem of retention.

There is also a quieter loss. Informal associations of volunteers have long been places where people who would never meet at work learn to cooperate, argue and decide things together. A committee that argues for an entire evening over the date of a jumble sale is, among other things, rehearsing the arts of compromise and accountability on which larger institutions depend. When decisions are taken by paid staff and volunteers are slotted into predefined roles, that practice of self-government shrinks. The organisation may deliver its service more reliably while doing less to cultivate the habits that made voluntary life worth defending.

None of this is an argument against training or rules as such. A rescue team on a mountain cannot depend on whoever turns up with good intentions, and anyone who works with children ought to be checked. The difficulty arises when standards suited to such demanding tasks are applied across the board, to the allotment society and the neighbourhood library as much as to the lifeboat crew. The sensible question is not whether to professionalise but where, and the answer should depend on what the task requires rather than on what funders find easy to count.

passage: In most human groups some people are listened to more than others, get their way more often and receive a larger share of whatever the group values. Students of status have long suspected that this single word conceals two different arrangements. In one, a person rises because others fear him: he can hurt them, withhold what they need or make their lives difficult, and they defer in order to avoid those costs. In the other, a person rises because others want something from him that he gives freely, usually knowledge or skill, and they defer in order to stay close enough to learn. The first route is commonly called dominance and the second prestige, and an influential line of thought in evolutionary anthropology holds that the second is a distinctively human addition to an older primate inheritance.

The argument for that view rests on the peculiar importance of cultural learning in our species. A creature that acquires most of its survival skills by copying others faces a constant problem of whom to copy, and a strong incentive to secure access to the best models. Deference, on this account, is a kind of payment: the learner offers attention, praise, small services and a willingness to yield in disputes, and in return is tolerated at the elbow of the skilled. If the account is right, it explains why prestige is freely conferred rather than extracted, why prestigious people are approached rather than avoided, and why we find ourselves imitating not only what admired people do well but much else about them besides.

That last consequence deserves more attention than it usually receives, because it shows that prestige is not simply the benign twin of dominance. Imitation guided by prestige is broad and indiscriminate. A learner cannot always tell which of a successful person's habits are responsible for the success, and so tends to copy a bundle of them: the method, but also the dress, the opinions and the manner of speech. In a small community this overspill is cheap and may even be useful, since the bundle often travels together for good reasons. In a large society with mass media, it allows people who are prestigious in one domain to exert influence far outside it, and the deference they receive bears no relation to any competence they have in the matters on which they are now heeded.

There is a further complication. The two routes are clean in theory and tangled in practice. A person who gains prestige acquires allies, resources and a following, and these are exactly the instruments with which dominance is exercised; prestige can thus be converted into the power to coerce, and the conversion is not always visible to those who continue to admire. Conversely, a dominant figure may cultivate the outward marks of prestige, surrounding himself with displays of learning or generosity that make submission feel like admiration. Observers who ask simply whether a leader is feared or respected will often find that the honest answer is both.

None of this undermines the distinction; it is precisely because the two routes can be told apart in principle that their mixture in practice becomes something to look for. What it undermines is the comfortable assumption that a society which replaces dominance with prestige has thereby solved the problem of status. Prestige allocates influence according to perceived excellence, and perception can be managed. The practical question for any institution is therefore not whether it rewards prestige rather than force, which most modern institutions at least claim to do, but whether it keeps the deference people receive tied to the domain in which they have actually earned it.

passage: The textbook account of banking runs roughly as follows. Savers deposit money; a bank keeps a fraction of each deposit as reserves and lends out the rest; the borrower spends the loan, the recipient deposits it at another bank, which in turn lends out most of it, and so on, until the original deposit has been multiplied by a factor that depends on the fraction held back. On this account banks are intermediaries, passing the savings of some people on to the projects of others, and the quantity of money in an economy is ultimately governed by the central bank's control over the quantity of reserves.

As a description of what actually happens when a loan is made, this has the sequence backwards. A bank that approves a loan does not hand over notes taken from a vault of accumulated deposits; it credits the borrower's account with a new deposit, and the money the borrower then spends did not exist a moment earlier. Lending creates deposits rather than the reverse. What limits a lender is therefore not a pool of prior savings but its judgement of whether a loan will be repaid at a profit, the capital it must hold against possible losses, the demand from creditworthy borrowers, and the price at which it can obtain the reserves needed to settle payments with other banks, a price that the central bank sets through the rate of interest rather than through the quantity of reserves.

The textbook is not simply wrong. A single bank that lends freely will soon find its new deposits draining away as borrowers pay people who bank elsewhere, and it must then attract deposits or borrow reserves to cover the outflow; from the standpoint of one institution, lending does seem to require funding. The error lies in generalising from the single bank to the system. What is a drain for one bank is an inflow for another, and the system as a whole is constrained less by the deposits it has gathered than by the willingness of banks to lend and of borrowers to borrow.

The difference matters for policy. If the multiplier story were right, a central bank that supplied banks with abundant reserves would set off a roughly proportionate expansion of lending. On the alternative account, when borrowers are cautious and banks are worried about losses, additional reserves may simply sit unused, because nothing in the decision to lend was waiting for them. Arguments about why lending has stalled are then better directed at the demand for credit and the condition of banks' balance sheets than at the quantity of reserves.

A further implication is drawn less often. If banks merely passed on existing savings, the direction of their lending would be a secondary matter, a question of how efficiently funds that already exist are placed. If instead banks create money when they lend, then their decisions about whom to lend to determine what new purchasing power enters the economy, and where. A boom in lending against existing houses and a boom in lending to firms that build new things both enlarge the supply of money, yet they do very different things with it: the first mainly raises the price of what is already there, while the second adds to what there is. Banking, on this view, is not a neutral pipe between savers and borrowers but one of the principal means by which a society decides what its new money will be used for.

passage: Defenders of nudging, the practice of steering choices by altering how options are presented rather than by forbidding or taxing any of them, have a ready answer to the charge that it is manipulative. Someone, they point out, must decide which option on a form is pre-selected, which dish stands at eye level in a canteen and which paragraph of a letter comes first; since there is no presentation without some arrangement, the choice is not between influencing people and leaving them alone but between influencing them thoughtfully and influencing them carelessly. The argument is sound as far as it goes, and critics who speak as though an unarranged menu were available are attacking a position nobody holds.

Yet the argument from inevitability answers a weaker objection than the one that matters. What troubles the more careful critics is not that choice architects influence us, which is unavoidable, but that many of the most effective nudges work precisely to the extent that they go unnoticed. A default enrolment in a savings scheme succeeds partly because inertia keeps people where they were placed, but also because many never register that a decision was made on their behalf; a smaller plate reduces consumption chiefly when diners do not reflect that they have been served less. Influence of this sort does not engage the faculties by which people govern themselves, but routes around them.

One way to sharpen the worry is to ask whether a given nudge would survive disclosure. Suppose a canteen posted a notice explaining that fruit had been placed at the front because the management wanted employees to eat more of it. If the arrangement continues to work, its power did not depend on concealment, and it begins to look less like manipulation than like a reminder. If it stops working once explained, that is evidence that it relied on a gap between what people were doing and what they understood themselves to be doing, and an institution that relies on such gaps owes its public a justification that it cannot easily give in public.

The test is not decisive in every case, and it should not be mistaken for a general condemnation. Some nudges would plainly survive disclosure: a letter telling people that most of their neighbours pay their taxes on time would plausibly work whether or not recipients knew why it had been sent, since the information is itself the influence. Others might fail it for innocent reasons, because a disclosure can itself distract, or can provoke a reflexive contrariness that has nothing to do with the merits of the option. What the test accomplishes is to shift the debate from an unanswerable question, whether influence is present, to an answerable one, whether the influence could be avowed. That shift concedes to the defenders everything their best argument actually establishes, and withholds from them only what it never established.

passage: Astronomers cannot lay a measuring tape across the sky, and almost every distance beyond the nearest stars is therefore inferred rather than measured. The method is usually described as a ladder. At the bottom are stars close enough for their apparent shift against the background, as the earth travels around the sun, to be observed and converted into a distance by simple geometry. Among those stars are certain pulsating ones whose rhythm of brightening and fading is tied to their true brightness, so that once the rhythm has been timed, a comparison of true with apparent brightness yields a distance. Such stars can be picked out in nearby galaxies, where they in turn calibrate brighter markers still, among them a class of exploding stars that can be seen across a large part of the observable universe.

Critics of the ladder, and many popular accounts of it, dwell on its fragility. Every rung rests on the one beneath, so an error at the bottom is carried, and perhaps magnified, all the way to the top. A small mistake in the geometry of nearby stars would misplace the pulsating stars, which would misplace the exploding ones, which would in turn misplace the remote galaxies whose distances tell us how fast the universe is expanding. On this view the ladder is really a chain, and a chain is only as strong as its weakest link.

The image is apt, but only half of it. A chain fails at its weakest link because each link is tested by nothing except the load it bears. The rungs of the distance ladder are tested by one another. Wherever two methods can both be applied to the same objects, their answers ought to agree, and when they do not, the disagreement points to a fault in one of them. Several of the largest revisions of cosmic distances in the past century came about in just this way, when a comparison between overlapping rungs exposed a hidden assumption, such as the neglect of dust that dims starlight or the confusion of two kinds of pulsating star with one. Interdependence, in other words, is not only a route by which errors travel upward; it is also the means by which they are caught.

This is no reason for complacency. Cross-checks catch only the errors that differ between methods; a mistake shared by every rung, or built into a calibration on which all of them rely, would pass each comparison untouched. That is why the present disagreement between the expansion rate measured with the ladder and the rate inferred from observations of the early universe is taken so seriously. It may expose a flaw common to the ladder's rungs, or it may reveal something new about the cosmos itself. Either outcome would be informative, and the fact that the question can be posed so sharply is itself a tribute to how far the ladder has been tightened. A structure that could not be checked could never have produced a disagreement worth arguing about.

passage: Few scientific failures are held against a discipline as often as seismology's inability to say when the next large earthquake will strike. The public imagines that a sufficiently clever instrument, placed in the right fault zone, ought eventually to detect a warning sign, much as a barometer falls before a storm. Over the past century researchers have pursued many such signs, from changes in groundwater levels and gas emissions to swarms of small tremors and odd animal behaviour. Each has, at one time or another, appeared to precede a particular earthquake, and each has failed when tested against the many earthquakes that came without it and the many apparent warnings that were followed by nothing.

It is worth separating two activities that ordinary speech runs together. A prediction, in the sense the public wants, names a place, a magnitude and a narrow window of time: a strong earthquake near this town within the next week. A forecast states a probability over a longer period: a given chance of shaking above some level in this region within the next thirty years. The first remains beyond reach, and many seismologists suspect it may stay there, because whether a small rupture grows into a large one seems to depend on conditions deep in the crust that no instrument can survey in detail. The second is routine, and it is far from useless.

Forecasts are what building codes are written from. When engineers decide how strongly a hospital must be braced, or which soils are too loose to build on, they are acting on probabilities of exactly this kind. A city that has absorbed its long-term hazard into the way it builds has, in effect, already received the most valuable warning seismology can give, though nobody experiences it as a warning, since it arrives years before the event and asks for money rather than flight.

The objection that a probability is too vague to act on mistakes the kind of decision at stake. Few people would evacuate a city on the strength of a one-in-twenty chance spread over three decades, and nobody should. But a decision about whether to reinforce a school is not a decision about this week; it is a decision about the lifetime of a building, and over that lifetime a one-in-twenty chance is large. This does not mean that the search for warning signs should be abandoned, since a reliable one would save lives that codes cannot. It means that the discipline should not be judged by its failure at a task it may never accomplish while its success at a quieter task goes unremarked.

passage: Imagine being told, after a brief task in which you estimated the number of dots flashed on a screen, that you belong to the group of 'overestimators'. You never meet another member of your group; you do not know who they are; nothing hangs on the label. You are then asked to divide small sums of money between two anonymous people, one described as an overestimator and the other as an underestimator. Experiments built on this design, which came to be called the minimal group paradigm, found that people reliably gave a little more to members of their own arbitrary category. Some even preferred allocations that maximised the gap between the groups over allocations that would have given their own group more in absolute terms.

The result has often been read as a revelation about human nature. If a meaningless label is enough to produce favouritism, the argument runs, then tribalism must be wired into us, waiting for any pretext, and the deeper divisions of nation, religion and ethnicity are only this primitive tendency writ large. The reading is dramatic, but it outruns the evidence in two ways.

First, what the experiments mostly showed was favouritism, not hostility. Participants tilted rewards towards their own side, but they were generally reluctant to impose costs on the other side when the task was framed as distributing penalties rather than rewards. Giving one's own a little more is not the same as wishing the others harm, and a theory of intergroup conflict that treats the two as interchangeable will misunderstand both. Second, the favouritism itself may be less mindless than it looks. Several later studies suggested that it shrinks when participants are told that members of their group will not know how they allocated, as though people were partly acting on an expectation that their own side would reciprocate. On that account the label is not a trigger for blind loyalty but a cue about whom one is in a cooperative relationship with.

None of this makes the original finding trivial. It remains striking that so thin a basis for belonging should shape behaviour at all, and the speed with which people adopt a category as their own deserves to be taken seriously. But the lesson that follows is not the fatalistic one. If group membership can be conjured from a coin toss or a dot-counting task, then it can also be redrawn: categories that are learned so easily are not fixed, and identities that cut across existing divisions can be built by the same mechanism that builds divisions in the first place.

What the laboratory cannot tell us is why particular divisions in the world become bitter. Real groups have histories, grievances and competing claims on land, jobs and power, and a five-minute label carries none of these. The minimal group paradigm shows where the raw material of loyalty comes from; it does not show what turns that material into enmity.

passage: A common complaint about protest is that it inconveniences people who have done nothing wrong. Commuters are delayed, shops lose trade, ambulances must find another route. The complaint has some force, but it often hides an assumption that deserves to be questioned: that legitimate protest would cause no inconvenience at all. A march that nobody notices, held where nobody has to walk around it, is hardly a protest. Part of the point of gathering in public is to make a claim that others cannot easily ignore.

This is why disruption has always been close to the centre of democratic protest rather than at its edge. Groups without money, office or access to the press have few ways of placing an issue on the public agenda, and a temporary cost imposed on the wider community is one of them. Many causes now regarded as plainly just were first brought to public notice by people who were considered a nuisance, and their critics complained, in much the same terms as are heard today, that they had chosen the wrong methods and the wrong moment.

None of this means that any disruption is acceptable. The useful distinction is between disruption that seeks a hearing and disruption that seeks to impose an outcome. The first imposes a cost in order to make others pay attention; it accepts that, once they have paid attention, they may still disagree. The second tries to make it impossible for others to act on their own decision, for instance by preventing a lawful vote from taking place or by keeping people from a service they are entitled to use. Protest of the first kind is part of the argument on which democracy runs. Protest of the second kind substitutes pressure for persuasion, and a democracy can rightly limit it.

Proportion matters as well. A blockade that delays traffic for an afternoon is different from one that prevents a hospital from receiving supplies, even if both are aimed only at securing attention. Those who protest have a responsibility to choose methods whose costs bear some relation to the importance of what they are saying, and those who govern have a responsibility not to treat every inconvenience as an emergency. Neither responsibility can be reduced to a simple rule, and particular cases will always be argued over; but the alternative to such argument is worse. A society that tolerates no disruption at all has, in effect, decided that only those who already have a hearing deserve one.

passage: The names we give to periods of the past look like neutral conveniences, markers on a timeline that allow us to say roughly when something happened. In fact most of them are compressed arguments. 'The Middle Ages' is the clearest case. The phrase took hold among European writers who believed that they were reviving the learning of the ancient world after a long interruption, and who therefore saw the intervening thousand years as an interval, a middle that mattered chiefly as the gap between two moments of achievement. A period named in this way has been judged before it has been studied.

Generations of historians have since shown how little that judgement fits the evidence. The centuries in question saw the founding of universities, the building of great cathedrals, the elaboration of law and the slow growth of towns and trade; far from being an interruption, they laid much of the ground on which later achievements stood. Yet the name has survived the demolition of the view that produced it, and it continues to whisper that the period was something to be got through. Words outlast the arguments that coined them.

The difficulty grows when such a label is exported. To speak of a 'medieval' period in the history of a region far from Europe is to import a chronology built for one part of the world, with its own sense of what came before and after, and to invite the historian to look there for whatever the label suggests, such as a decline and a later rebirth, whether or not the evidence of that region points to anything of the kind.

It does not follow that we should try to do without period names. History cannot be written without some way of grouping years together, and the alternatives are not innocent either: centuries are as arbitrary as any label, cutting through lives and movements at points chosen by arithmetic, and they bring a peculiar habit of their own, the tendency to treat each hundred years as having a single character. The sensible course is to keep the names while holding them lightly, treating each as a hypothesis about what a stretch of time had in common, to be tested against the evidence and abandoned where it fails. The danger lies not in having labels but in letting the label arrive before the research and decide what the research will look for.

passage: When a person who keeps all her appointments in a phone loses the phone, she often says that she has lost her memory, and the phrase is less of an exaggeration than it sounds. For a growing number of thinkers, the boundary of the mind is not the skin or the skull but the reach of the processes that do a mind's work. If a notebook is consulted as automatically as recollection, trusted as fully and available as readily, then, the argument goes, the information it holds is as much a part of its owner's beliefs as anything stored in the brain. To insist otherwise is, on this view, a mere prejudice in favour of the inside.

The argument has real force, and much of it should be accepted. It is hard to say what principled difference there is between a fact that I must work to recall and a fact that I can retrieve, with less effort, from a list I always carry. Both are stored, both are retrieved, and both guide what I do. Ordinary practice already reflects this: we hold someone responsible for knowing what is written in the diary she relies on, and we speak of a shopping list as remembering things for us. When a skill depends on a tool, as a carpenter's feel for the wood depends on a plane he has used for years, the tool can seem less an object he handles than a part of how he perceives.

Yet the stronger conclusion, that the mind simply is whatever system includes the tool, moves too quickly. Devices differ from memory in a way the argument tends to pass over: they can be edited by other people. A notebook can be altered while its owner sleeps; the contents of a phone can be changed by whoever manages the service on which it depends. Biological memory is fallible, and it too can be distorted by suggestion, but it is not open in the same routine way to the revisions of strangers. The difference is not one of storage but of authority, of who has the standing to change what a person takes to be true.

The better lesson, then, is not that minds are everywhere but that trust has become a part of cognition. Once we lean on external stores, the question of whether our beliefs are sound becomes partly a question about the institutions and people who maintain those stores. That is why the loss, or the quiet alteration, of a device can feel like an injury to the self and not merely an inconvenience. The thesis that the mind extends into its tools is right to notice the injury; it is wrong to think that calling the device a part of the mind explains it.

passage: We tend to think of the weekend as a natural feature of the calendar, as if two days of rest had always followed five of work. In fact the arrangement is fairly recent, and its history suggests that free time is not simply the absence of work but something that has to be made, defended and shaped. Before the factory, many artisans worked in bursts, labouring late into the night to finish an order and then taking a day or two off whenever it suited them; in parts of England the habit of stretching Sunday's rest into Monday was common enough to be given a mock saint's name, 'Saint Monday'.

Factory production could not tolerate this irregularity. Machines were expensive and had to run whenever the hands were present, and an employer could not plan production around workers who might drift in on Tuesday, so the long struggle over hours was therefore also a struggle over the shape of time. Workers wanted fewer hours; employers wanted predictable ones. The compromise that eventually emerged, first a half-day on Saturday and later the whole of it, gave each side part of what it sought. Workers won rest that was guaranteed rather than snatched, and employers won a workforce that turned up, sober, on Monday morning.

It would be wrong to see the outcome merely as a defeat dressed up as a victory. For most working people, guaranteed free time was a real gain, and it was won against resistance. But the weekend also changed what free time was. Leisure that had once been taken at the worker's discretion became a fixed block, the same for everyone, and a block that was the same for everyone could be sold to. Football matches, excursion trains and seaside resorts arranged themselves around Saturday afternoon and Sunday, and leisure came increasingly to mean something one went out and paid for at a scheduled time.

The lesson is not that the old irregular rhythm was better; it was often tied to poverty, to insecurity and to binges of overwork that left people exhausted. It is that arguments about working hours are never only about quantity. When people today argue over flexible schedules or a four-day week, they are reopening a question that the industrial age settled in one particular way: not merely how much time should be free, but who decides when it falls and what it is for.

passage: It is tempting to picture the great periodic fair of the pre-modern world as a market that happened to be very large. Merchants arrived with bales of cloth, casks and livestock; buyers came from the surrounding districts; for a few weeks a meadow outside a town became a crowded street of stalls, and then it emptied again until the following year. On this view the fair existed because trade was too thin to support permanent shops, and it faded once towns grew large enough to sustain them. The account is not wrong, but it describes the visible part of the fair and mistakes it for the whole.

Much of what happened at a fair left no bales behind. Merchants who met there once or twice a year used the occasion to settle accounts that had been running since the previous meeting, cancelling what one owed another against what a third owed the first, so that relatively little coin had to change hands. Promises to pay at the next fair circulated as a kind of credit, and their value rested on the expectation that everyone would return. A fair, in this sense, was a calendar as much as a place: it fixed the dates on which obligations fell due and gave distant traders a reason to keep faith with one another. A merchant who failed to appear risked more than a season's sales; he risked his standing with every partner who had expected to meet him.

It was also a clearing house for news. Prices in distant regions, the solvency of a trading house, a harvest failure, rumours of war: all of this travelled with the people who came, and a merchant who stayed at home was not only missing customers but trading blind. The gossip of the fair was not idle. It was the means by which a scattered commercial world kept a rough common picture of itself. A thinly attended fair was therefore a loss twice over, since the absence of buyers was also an absence of reports, and those who controlled the best information often profited more than those who carried the most goods.

Seen this way, the decline of the great fairs looks different. Permanent shops certainly took over much of the retail business, but the deeper loss was of the fair's other functions, which passed to institutions that did not depend on bodily presence: banks that kept accounts all year round, regular postal services and, later, printed lists of prices. None of this means that fairs ceased to matter as markets; many survived for centuries as places to buy animals or household goods. What they lost was their role as the hinge on which a whole year of commerce turned, and that role had never been visible in the stalls.

passage: Elections are so closely identified with democracy that it can seem perverse to ask whether they are democratic at all. Yet consider what an election rewards. To win, a candidate must stand out from the crowd: be better known, better funded, better connected or simply more persuasive on a platform than the people whose votes are sought. An election is, in this sense, a procedure for picking a distinguished few, and the chambers it fills tend to resemble the electorate less closely than a random sample of that electorate would. Many ancient Greek writers saw the point clearly; for them, filling offices by lot was the characteristically democratic method, and election was a device that favoured the prominent.

The modern case for selection by lot builds on that old intuition. A body drawn at random from the adult population brings into the room the people who are usually spoken about rather than heard: the shift worker, the pensioner, the young parent who would never run for anything. Its members owe nothing to donors or to party managers, since nobody campaigned to put them there. Above all, they are free to change their minds. An elected representative who revises a position after hearing the evidence risks being called a turncoat; a citizen chosen by lot has no platform to betray, and so can treat a question as something to be worked out rather than a position to be defended.

Critics usually reply that ordinary citizens lack the competence to legislate. This objection is weaker than it sounds. Few elected legislators are experts in more than a sliver of what they vote on; they rely on staff, committees and witnesses, and there is no reason a randomly chosen body could not do the same. A more serious difficulty concerns accountability. An elected member who disappoints can be removed at the next election, and the prospect of removal disciplines conduct in between. A member chosen by lot answers to no one, and the very independence that shields such a member from donors also shields him or her from voters. Those who propose replacing elected chambers with lotteries have not, to my mind, answered this objection.

The sensible conclusion is not that lot should displace election but that it can do something election does badly. On some questions elected politicians have every incentive to avoid committing themselves, because any clear answer will cost them votes. A panel chosen at random, given time, evidence and a duty to hear opposing witnesses, can show what ordinary people conclude once they have actually thought the matter through, and its recommendations can then be put to the legislature or to the voters for decision. The lottery's virtue is that it reveals considered public judgement; its limit is that no one has authorised the people it selects to rule.

passage: The sceptical argument about induction, usually traced to David Hume, has a disarming simplicity. Every inference from observed cases to unobserved ones assumes that the future will resemble the past, or more generally that nature is uniform. That assumption cannot be proved by logic, since its denial involves no contradiction, and it cannot be supported by experience without circularity, since the support would itself be an inference from observed cases. Philosophers have spent a long time looking for a way out, usually by searching for a single principle that would license inductive inference in general.

The search may be misconceived, because there is no such thing as inductive inference in general. Consider two investigators. One measures the melting point of a newly prepared sample of a pure compound and concludes, from a single careful trial, that every sample of that compound will melt at the same temperature. Another measures the height of one adult and draws no conclusion at all about the heights of adults. Both are reasoning well, and they differ not because one has found the universal principle and the other has not, but because each knows something about the kind of thing being studied: that pure compounds are uniform in their melting points, and that people are not uniform in their heights.

On this picture, what licenses an inductive step is not a principle of uniformity but particular facts about particular domains, which tell us how far a sample can be trusted to stand in for the whole. The obvious objection is that this merely relocates the problem. Our confidence that compounds are uniform in their melting points was itself acquired by induction, and so the sceptic can ask what licenses that.

The objection is fair, but it is less damaging than it looks, because it trades on an ambiguity between justifying each belief and justifying all of them together. The regress it describes is real, yet it never requires us to justify all our inductive habits at once. At any moment we lean on some background knowledge in order to test some other part of it, and any item can in turn be questioned while the rest is held fixed. This does not answer the sceptic on the sceptic's own terms, which demand a foundation lying outside experience altogether. It does show that the demand is not one that science, as actually practised, needs to meet in order to be rational, any more than a household needs to audit every account on the same afternoon in order to keep honest books.

passage: Egalitarians hold that there is something wrong with inequality as such: that when some people are much worse off than others through no fault of their own, the situation is bad, and bad in part simply because of the gap. The most famous objection to this view asks us to consider what follows from it. Suppose that the only way to remove an inequality were to make the better off worse off, with no benefit to anyone, as if a town in which some households had gardens and others had none could reach equality only by paving over every garden. If inequality is bad in itself, then such a change would remove something bad, and so would be in one respect an improvement. Yet the change helps no one and harms many. To call it an improvement in any respect, the objectors say, is absurd.

Many philosophers have been moved by this objection to give up equality as a fundamental value. Some have adopted the view that benefits matter more the worse off their recipient is, so that a gain to a poor person counts for more than the same gain to a rich one; others hold that what matters is that everyone should have enough, after which differences cease to be of moral concern. Neither view is troubled by levelling down, since on neither does reducing the well-being of the better off, by itself, improve anything. Both also capture much of what drew people to equality in the first place, which was a concern for those who are badly off.

Yet the objection is less decisive than it is usually taken to be. The egalitarian need not claim that a levelled-down world is better all things considered, only that it is better in one respect while much worse in others. Plural values often pull apart in this way. We can think that a promise kept at terrible cost was in one respect admirable without thinking that it should have been kept. Seen this way, the levelling-down case shows only that equality is not the only thing that matters, which almost no egalitarian ever believed.

This defence succeeds, but at a price. It keeps equality as a value only by making it a strangely impersonal one: something that can make a state of affairs better while making it better for no one at all. Many will find such a value hard to care about. There is, however, another way to understand what egalitarians were after. On a relational view, the core of equality lies not in how goods are distributed but in how people stand to one another: in the absence of rank, servility and contempt, in a society where no one must bow and no one may command another merely by virtue of birth or wealth. Inequalities of resources matter on this view chiefly because, beyond some point, they turn into inequalities of standing, as when wealth buys influence over others or poverty forces deference to them.

The relational view is untouched by the levelling-down objection, because paving over gardens neither creates nor abolishes any relation of rank between neighbours. Whether it can say enough about distribution is a further question. A society might abolish titles and deference while leaving vast differences in income intact, and the relational egalitarian owes us an account of when such differences begin to corrode equal standing. But the view has at least located the value of equality in a relation between persons, which is where most of its defenders always felt it to be.

passage: It has become a commonplace that every age describes the brain in the image of its most impressive machine. When ornamental gardens were fitted with water-driven statues that moved as visitors stepped on hidden plates, nerves were pictured as pipes and the animal spirits as fluid pressed through them. When the telegraph and then the telephone exchange spread across cities, the nervous system became a network of wires, with the brain as the central office where calls were connected. In our own time it is a computer, processing information, storing memories and running programs. The pattern is real, and critics have drawn a sharp lesson from it: the metaphors are fashions, each as quaint as the last will soon appear, and the computer image will go the way of the fountain.

The lesson is half right. It is true that none of these images was the whole truth, and that each looks dated once the technology behind it is familiar. But to call them mere fashions is to miss what each one got right. The hydraulic picture captured the idea that something must travel from the senses to the centre and back to the muscles. The switchboard captured the importance of connections, of which signal is routed to which destination. The computer captured the idea that what matters about these signals is the information they carry and the transformations performed on it, rather than the stuff that carries them. Each metaphor, in other words, was adopted because it made some feature of the nervous system thinkable, and each left behind a contribution that survived its own retirement.

The real danger lies elsewhere, because a metaphor brings with it not only the features that fit but a whole set of features that come along unexamined. The computer image invites us to think of memory as storage, a place where a record sits unchanged until retrieved, when remembering appears to be closer to reconstruction, the record altered a little each time it is used. It invites a sharp division between hardware and software, when in the brain the program and the machine are hard to tell apart, since use reshapes the very structures that do the work. These are not reasons to abandon the metaphor but reasons to keep asking which of its features we are actually entitled to.

The sensible course, then, is neither to treat the current metaphor as a literal description nor to dismiss it as a passing fashion, but to use it while keeping an account of where it fails. Metaphors are tools for thinking about something that cannot be seen directly, and the history of brain science suggests that thinking without any of them is not an available option. What can be avoided is the habit of mistaking the tool for the thing.

passage: Suppose you and a colleague whom you regard as your equal in competence and care examine the same evidence and reach opposite conclusions. Neither of you has information the other lacks; neither has reason to think the other was tired or distracted. What should you do? An influential answer holds that you should move towards your colleague's view, giving her opinion the same weight as your own. The thought behind it is simple. From a neutral standpoint, the disagreement is evidence that one of you has erred, and you have no reason, independent of the dispute itself, to think the error is hers rather than yours. To stand firm would be to treat the mere fact that a conclusion is yours as a reason to favour it.

This principle seems to me correct over a wide range of cases, and it is more demanding than most people find comfortable. It condemns the familiar move of discounting a dissenter precisely because she dissents: 'she is usually so sensible, but on this question she has plainly lost her way'. If the only evidence that she has lost her way is that she disagrees with you, the reasoning simply assumes what is in question.

Yet the principle cannot be applied without qualification. Imagine two equally able auditors reviewing the same short ledger, one of whom concludes that the accounts balance while the other reports that the firm's assets exceed the number of grains of sand on the earth. The first auditor need not split the difference. Her confidence that her colleague has blundered does not rest on her own conclusion about the ledger; it rests on the absurdity of his, which she can recognise without relying on the reasoning they disagree about. What licenses holding firm, then, is not that a view is one's own but that one has grounds, independent of the dispute, for locating the error on the other side. The equal-weight principle survives, but it turns out to be a claim about what to do when such independent grounds are absent, not a rule that applies whatever one knows.

Critics sometimes press a further objection: since thoughtful people disagree about the equal-weight principle itself, the principle seems to require its own defenders to lose confidence in it. This is less damaging than it first appears. A principle about how to respond to disagreement may well recommend reduced confidence in itself without thereby becoming false; it would show only that the matter is genuinely hard, which no one denied. What the objection does reveal is that conciliation cannot be the whole story about rational belief. A thinker who revised every view the moment a peer dissented would soon have no settled views left to revise, and some account is still owed of what entitles anyone to a starting point.
